newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA DOMESTIC DEBT UP AT 668 BLN LEVS IN OCT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA DOMESTIC DEBT UP AT 668 BLN LEVS IN OCT.

text.p: Bulgaria's domestic debt rose by 27.7 billion levs in October to 668.3 billion levs due to new issues of government securities and a fall of the national currency, the lev, Finance Ministry figures showed.
Nine new treasury paper issues were sold last month to finance the government budget deficit, boosting domestic debt by 10.8 billion levs, figures showed.

Another 10 billion levs added to the debt due to the lev fall from 230 to 240 against the dollar in October, which boosted the price of dollar-denominated bad loan bonds and treasury bonds issued to compensate depositors in insolvent banks.
This year the Finance Ministry issued $61 million worth of floater coupon T-bonds to guarantee hard currency deposits in banks which the central bank seeks to close down.

Direct credit to the government from the central bank, the State Savings Bank and State Insurance Institute rose from 42.4 billion levs in September to 49.4 billion levs in October, boosting domestic debt by another seven billion levs.
The Finance Ministry has recently said it planned to meet most maturity and coupon payments on treasury papers by rollover issues of government securities to bridge the budget gap.
The central government budget deficit topped the annual target by nine percent in October, rising to 88 billion levs.
Discussions about the introduction of a currency board system in Bulgaria proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have raised deep concerns among banks, a commercial banker told Reuters.
"Some banks are trying to get rid of treasury paper in their portfolios through buy-back operations with the central bank ahead of maturity," said the banker, who declined to be named.

Banks authorised to sell treasury paper to individuals and firms were under pressure to buy it back ahead of maturity as Bulgarians feared for the safety of their lev-denominated investments if a currency board system was introduced.
Individuals and non-banking institutions held 61.4 billion levs worth of paper at the end of October or 23.4 percent of the total par value of issues in circulation.
Issueing and servicing of bad loan bonds amounted to some 80 percent of the total internal debt, the finance ministry said in a report made available to Reuters.
"State companies' bad debts should have been covered by sales of their assets and it is still possible through speeding up of privatisation," the report said.
Bulgaria issued two types of bad debt bonds in 1994 and 1995 worth 32 billion levs and $1.8 billion respectively to cover banks' non-performing loans extended to state companies before 1991.
"It is highly advisable to encourage debt-for-equity swaps to cut the domestic debt and to stop the transfer of company losses to the state," the report said.
Finance Ministry officials were not available for further comment.
